title: Why are so many men obsessed with “disproving” feminist movies like Barbie?

commenti.body: [removed]

The kind of men who make these arguments hate women. And since they hate women, they cannot accept that women are equal. So in order to preserve their worldview that women are less than men, they make it their mission to "dismantle" feminist themes in the media they consume.

[removed]

I feel like the answer to this question is fairly obvious, lol. Because it challenges their worldview and confronts the consequences of that in such a way that forces you to empathize with the characters. 

I’ve talked a lot about how Gerwig attempts to decontruct and divorce gender inequality from gender in this film, mostly successfully, and how she reconstructs it back at the end of the film, to really seal the message. I think this is one of the reasons the film is so successful and has resonated with a lot of people, regardless of gender, but I could “understand” how specific pockets of men would feel totally alienated by this. 

My personal pet peeve with this film is less that it’s getting bad faith flack, it’s that so much praise comes with a caveat at the top. It’s a fun, interesting film! I don’t want to have to pre-address all the criticisms that I anticipate coming my way when I talk about why I love it.

Does engaging with a piece of art entail uncritical agreement with whatever it, its creators, or you in particular have to say about it? Can you name other groups you hold to that standard, or other kinds of art you similarly deem exempt from criticism?

For the same reason ratings on IMDB (just as one instance) are unrealistically low on almost any movie perceived as feminist or displaying a minimum of positivity toward women etc. Or, think of the madness that was brigading Hollywood blockbusters when they dared open up lead roles to women and similar, piling abuse on actors and even chasing them off social media.

Misogyny. It won't be eradicated for a while yet...

Sometimes it’s hard to tell what’s gaslighting and what are legitimately held beliefs. A female director releasing a popular movie that destroys at the box office and another male director who releases a movie at the exact same time but gets 1/10 of the criticism, and Oppenheimer was worthy of it, is pretty sus to me.

Because they have to put any movie that appeals to women down. They think women are inferior to men. So art made for women is inferior to art made for men.

For me personally I honestly prefer this to almost any big blockbuster movie to come out in the last 10 or so years. Not saying it's perfect or anything but it's cool to see a super popular movie actually have a personality for once and not be complete garbage.

Yeah I really loved it. I loved will Ferrell and the corporate scenes as well. There was a thread here where some users were already pronouncing it as “having no cultural impact” and I’m like…dude  I’m a guy and even I can tell this is gonna be a generational film for women.

Same as how Mean Girls was for girls/women in the 2000’s. The only difference being people weren’t dressing up in flamboyant pink to see mean girls because it was a social event.

Nice response. But the OP asked about Barbie and feminism, not about other movies or their subject matter.

Can you answer their question, which is specifically about Barbie and feminism? 

And where did they say Barbie was exempt from criticism? They never said that. Your non-answer speaks volumes. 

My answer would be that certain men, are threatened because they feel that men are being used as a scapegoat. These men can't find the humor in the situations because they take the film too seriously, which is something that wasn't intended. 90% of men can laugh and enjoy the movie, the remaining 10% take the film as a personal attack, or worse a false premise.
Lol as evidenced by the meatheads in this sub downvoting.

I personally don't like Barbie because I think it's a bastardization of a revolutionary ideology (feminism) so that it can serve capitalism.
Having said that, I think most men hate this kind of film because, firstly, they hate being in the presence of media aimed primarily at a female audience. So when a film of this kind reaches such a high level of popularity, they feel that it's being imposed on them, because in their minds, neutrality = media made for men.
Secondly, the female perspective is not something they value enough to find any interest in this kind of film.
And thirdly, despite all the progress made, feminism is still an ideology that many men take a dim view of, because it implies that they are oppressors and part of the problem, so they need to do some introspection to understand what they're doing wrong and improve. Problem is, people hate to question themselves and hate to be confronted with the idea that they have privilege.
You add all this to the immense number of people consuming Red Pill content every day...

Yeah, I have some thoughts. Particularly at the moment because a couple of days ago one of these guys took issue with me saying that Birds of Prey was one of my favourite action movies and that I thought it was great. He accused me of only liking it because it's "pretty" (his use of quotation marks not mine) and then told me the only real reason I could possibly have for holding these opinions was that I was pushing some kind of nefarious agenda. Sadly he blocked me after I called him a sad, sad man and I didn't have a chance to screenshot the nonsense before it all disappeared.

I think a lot of hetero, cis, white men don't have a lot of resilience when it comes to things not being for them. They're used to lobbing up to the movies and being spoilt for choice for films that are for and about them, and that represent them. And not only is this movie not written for them, but it's wildly popular and people are raving about it!!?? Something must have gone terribly wrong with the world! (Nb 'not for them' meaning they are not the target audience, I know a bunch of hetero, cis, white men who thoroughly enjoyed it, despite not being the target audience).
Oppenheimer wasn’t a cultural criticism. Barbie was - it is more controversial and should be more controversial because it was written to challenge people rather than serve as a biography.

I think this is kind of a loaded question as I feel like it presumes a conclusion rather than asking what the possibilities of an idea are.

As someone who is male, I am embarrassed by the replacement narrative that having different genders have the same type of agency as what male-driven cinema has been for the past 80 years is some type of censorship.

On the flipside, I do think it is a bit interrogative and not intrinsic to demand a film educate the audience of the tenants of feminism.

But the thing there is that they'll always be a sexist trolls and people who gather around the word woke to blur the forest and trees together.

I think that audience kind of looks for things to dislike.
I think to their logic, but if a woman is powerful, she's a Mary Sue, if she's weak, she's useless, and if she's normal.. she's considered uninteresting.

With Barbie, it was always going to be a toy commercial.

Hey, this is also true for The Lego Movie.

The thing is with characters of their nature, their main job is to sell toys, so they are more plastic saints then dynamic. 

But I always think that film theorists who consider a belief system as a grounds for appreciation or dislike kind of remind me of my boomer friends rummaging  media for Saranic content. If you look for the devil, you will find him.

Eh, the movie is unrealistic when it comes to women being treated by men in 2023. I would understand if we were living in the 1950s and the cultural toxic masculine ideals are something we still honored. But fortunately, we don't honor those cultural ideals because it's 2023 lol. I get that there's still a hatred and disillusionment for men from a large amount of women because of how women were treated in the past by some men (and so the movie feeds that and entertains them) but because it's trying to create the idea that it's 1950 in 2023 it just comes off as unrealistic and jarring.

I haven't seen Barbie, so I can't comment on anything specific to that film, but I take umbrage with the all-too-pervasive notion that even outright contrarian views cannot be arrived at sincerely and must be coming from some moral failure.

When you use art to convey a message there will be people that disagree with that message. If not, then what is even the point of creating the film in the first place? It should be thought provoking and create discussion if the goal of the film is to do so. 

Point A is obvious why it is being attacked by a certain group - beliefs fundamentally disagree with the message the movie is trying to convey. That doesn’t make them right and most people don’t agree with them (hence the overwhelming praise the movie has gotten) but it’s pretty clear why they don’t like it. 

Point B is trickier and it’s more of an attack on Hollywood in general. There is a small but vocal group that is very against neoliberal values and so it doesn’t like how the movie uses materialistic and corporate ideas to deliver its message. They see it as a corporation buying favor in the eyes of the public to look like they’re the good guys.

Both these groups need to exist or else the theme of the movie would be boring and pointless with nothing to discuss. The beauty is how artists can use film to tackle controversial ideas and distribute them to a wide audience. Without that controversy there would be nothing to discuss, just like how there isn’t much to discuss in cookie cutter super hero films that are about an obvious good and obvious evil.

I saw a lot of criticism directed at Oppenheimer for not including the Japanese perspective. I have also seen a tremendous amount of criticism of Barbie from feminists who deride it as a corporate advertisement that refuses to critically examine the product it’s selling.

>Does engaging with a piece of art...

Honestly, I'm fine with criticizing Barbie as not being "high art" and suggesting it doesn't deserve to be nominated for a bunch of awards or whatever... but let's be real:  the vast majority of criticism didn't stem from how much artistic value it had...

Most of the criticism came from the same place that had the world hating the all-women Ghostbusters or 2018 Overboard or Ocean's 8 or anything else which... wasn't exactly the "high art."

If we're talking artistic value then it shouldn't be judged better or worse simply because of the subject matter.  That is all.

Like, I don't care how much you love America and patriotism... Rocky IV is just not the greatest film ever made...

Similarly, I don't care how much you hate "wokeness" - Barbie wasn't "garbage."

If you have biases/prejudices that heavily influence your subjective opinions?  I even get that!  Everyone does.  That's normal.  But reasonable people can appreciate that.

I'm very fond of terrible Sword & Sorcery films and tend to be very unappreciative of disaster movies.  Are Conan or Scorpion King great films?  Probably not... I'm just very biased.  Are Titanic and The Impossible great films?  Probably... but I'm very biased.
